sections.title: A chariot of stone that sailors steered by
sections.intro_md:
Around **1250 CE**, King **Narasimhadeva I** of the Eastern Ganga dynasty built a temple to the Sun on the beach at Konark. It was designed as Surya's chariot: **24 carved stone wheels**, **seven stone horses**, and a tower that may have stood about **70 m** high, taller than any building in Odisha would be for 700 years.

The tower was so dark and so tall that European sailors used it as a landmark. By **1676** their charts called it the **Black Pagoda**, and Puri's whitewashed Jagannath temple, 35 km down the coast, the White Pagoda. The sea has since retreated, and the great tower is gone: it had collapsed by the 19th century. What you see today is only the porch, the jagamohana, and even that was packed with sand and sealed by the British in **1903** to stop it falling in.

That is Odisha in one site. A coast that once sent ships to Bali, a dynasty rich enough to carve a chariot from a hillside of stone, and a heritage that survived on stubbornness and sand.

spotlights.name: Konark Sun Temple
spotlights.when: Built about 1250 CE; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984
spotlights.spot_it: A squat black stone hall on a high plinth ringed with giant wheels, horses at the front, no tower.
spotlights.story_md: Every surface is carved: elephants, musicians, wrestlers, giraffe-like animals, couples, court scenes and dancers mid-step on the roof terraces. The stone is mostly **khondalite**, which weathers dark. The temple was aligned so the first light of dawn struck the sanctum. Its main tower fell long ago; the cause is debated, from weak foundations on sandy ground to damage in later wars. The surviving jagamohana is still about 39 m tall. **Rabindranath Tagore** wrote that here the language of stone surpasses the language of man. UNESCO listed it in **1984**, and it is on the back of the brown ₹10 note issued from 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the high point of Kalinga temple architecture and the state's best-known image.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Black Pagoda: a lighthouse that was really a chariot for the Sun.

spotlights.name: The Konark wheel
spotlights.spot_it: A stone wheel about 3 m across with 8 thick spokes and 8 thin ones, every rim crowded with carving.
spotlights.story_md: There are 24 wheels, 12 pairs, often read as the months or the hours of day and night. Guides at Konark lay a finger across a spoke and read the time from its shadow, and the wheels are widely described as sundials accurate to minutes. Whether the builders meant them as clocks is not proven, but the shadow trick works well enough to amaze visitors. The wheel has become India's design shorthand: in September 2023 world leaders at the G20 summit in New Delhi were welcomed in front of a giant Konark wheel backdrop.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A 13th-century carving is now a national symbol of time and motion.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-four stone wheels, and a shadow you can tell the time by.

sections.title: Odisha at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Odisha sits on India's east coast between West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh, with Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh inland. It covers **155,707 km²**, the 8th largest state, about the size of Bangladesh, and had **4.20 crore** people in Census 2011, 11th in India. About **82.7%** speak Odia; about **93.6%** are Hindu.

It was the first Indian province drawn on the basis of language, on **1 April 1936**, celebrated as **Utkal Divas**. The capital moved from Cuttack to a new planned city, **Bhubaneswar**, in 1948. In **November 2011** the English spelling changed from Orissa to **Odisha**, and the language from Oriya to **Odia**, to match how people actually say them.

The numbers that matter: a coastline of roughly 480 km facing the cyclone-prone Bay of Bengal; **30 districts**; **62 Scheduled Tribes**, more than any other state, making up about **22.8%** of the people; and some of the richest mineral land in Asia, with most of India's chromite and a large share of its bauxite and iron ore. In 2024 the state changed government for the first time in 24 years.

spotlights.name: Bhubaneswar
spotlights.spot_it: Wide planned avenues on one side, a dense old town of sandstone temple towers around a large tank on the other.
spotlights.story_md: Bhubaneswar is two cities. The old one, **Ekamra Kshetra**, grew around the Bindu Sagar tank; tradition says it once had 7,000 temples, and hundreds still stand, built over about 1,200 years. The new one was planned from 1948 by the German architect **Otto Koenigsberger**, who had been chief architect of Mysore state. Nehru laid its foundation stone in April 1948. In 2016 Bhubaneswar came first in India's national Smart Cities Challenge, and it hosted the men's hockey World Cups of 2018 and 2023. Locals still call it the Temple City.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Odisha's two faces at once: ancient pilgrimage town and planned modern capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bhubaneswar: 7,000 temples in legend, one German planner in fact.

sections.title: Delta, lagoon and hills
sections.intro_md:
Odisha has three bands. Along the coast lies a flat, fertile **delta** built by the Mahanadi, Brahmani and Baitarani, where most people live and rice grows. Inland rise the **Eastern Ghats** and the Chota Nagpur plateau edge, forested and mineral-rich, where most tribal communities live. Between them are river valleys and rolling uplands. The highest point is **Deomali**, about 1,672 m, in Koraput.

The **Mahanadi**, 'the great river', drains much of Chhattisgarh and Odisha before reaching the sea near Paradip. It floods often; in western Odisha it is held back by the Hirakud Dam. The coast is low, and that makes it both rich and dangerous. Long beaches suit nesting turtles and fishing villages, and the shallow shelf of the Bay of Bengal lets cyclone storm surges reach far inland.

The great coastal water body is **Chilika**, a lagoon of salt and fresh water joined to the sea by a narrow mouth. Forest covers about a third of the state.

spotlights.name: Chilika Lake

where.label: Chilika Lake, Puri, Khordha and Ganjam districts

spotlights.spot_it: A vast, shallow, pale lagoon dotted with fishing boats, islands and stake nets, the sea just beyond a sand bar.
spotlights.story_md: Chilika is Asia's largest brackish-water lagoon, about 64 km long and roughly 900 to 1,165 km² depending on the season. In winter around a million migratory birds arrive, many from Central Asia and Siberia, crowding the **Nalabana** island sanctuary. By the 1990s silt had choked the mouth, salinity fell, weeds spread and fish catches crashed; in 1993 it was put on the Ramsar 'Montreux Record' of threatened wetlands. In **2000** engineers cut a new mouth to the sea. Fish and prawn returned, and in **2002** Chilika became the first site in Asia taken off the Montreux Record. About two lakh fishers depend on it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare case where a damaged wetland was measurably fixed.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chilika: one new mouth in 2000, and a dying lagoon breathed again.

spotlights.name: Hirakud Dam
spotlights.spot_it: A long low earthen embankment with a concrete spillway, curving across the Mahanadi near Sambalpur.
spotlights.story_md: Hirakud was one of independent India's first big multipurpose river projects, built to tame Mahanadi floods, irrigate western Odisha and make power. Including its dykes it runs about **25.8 km**, among the longest earthen dams in the world, and its reservoir became one of the largest artificial lakes in Asia. Nehru poured the first concrete in 1948 and opened it in 1957. The cost was human as well: hundreds of villages went under water, and tens of thousands of displaced people waited decades for full compensation. In dry summers, the ruins of drowned temples reappear above the water.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It brought water and power to the west, and set the pattern for India's debates on displacement.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hirakud: 25.8 km of earth, and temples that surface when the lake runs low.

sections.title: Turtles, dolphins, crocodiles and black tigers
sections.intro_md:
Odisha's coast and forests hold four animal stories that most of the world does not know belong to India.

On a few beaches, hundreds of thousands of **olive ridley turtles** come ashore together to nest, a spectacle seen in only a handful of places on Earth. In Chilika live **Irrawaddy dolphins**, a round-headed river and lagoon dolphin. In the mangroves of **Bhitarkanika**, India's second-largest mangrove forest after the Sundarbans, a crocodile project begun in 1975 has rebuilt the largest population of **saltwater crocodiles** in India. And in **Similipal**, a tiger reserve in Mayurbhanj, a third or more of the tigers carry a gene that makes their stripes merge into black.

All four depend on people choosing to leave them alone: fishing bans at nesting time, dolphin-safe boat rules, and a reserve where villagers live beside tigers.

spotlights.name: Olive ridley arribada

where.label: Gahirmatha, Rushikulya and Devi river mouth

spotlights.when: Mass nesting, usually February to April
spotlights.spot_it: A beach covered at night by small olive-grey turtles, flippers flinging sand, hundreds in sight at once.
spotlights.story_md: The Spanish word **arribada**, 'arrival', names the event: females gather offshore, then come ashore in their thousands over a few nights. Odisha has three such beaches, **Gahirmatha**, the **Rushikulya** river mouth and the **Devi** river mouth, and Gahirmatha is often called the largest known rookery in the world. In good years several lakh turtles nest; Rushikulya alone recorded close to seven lakh nests in 2025. Each lays around 100 eggs. Sand temperature decides the sex: warmer nests make females. Trawler nets drowned more than 100,000 ridleys off Odisha between 1993 and 2003, which is why fishing is now banned near the beaches in season.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Odisha hosts one of the largest sea-turtle nestings on the planet.
spotlights.memory_hook: Arribada: hot sand makes daughters, cool sand makes sons.

spotlights.name: Irrawaddy dolphin
spotlights.spot_it: A grey dolphin with a blunt, rounded forehead, no beak and a small stubby fin, surfacing quietly.
spotlights.story_md: *Orcaella brevirostris* lives in a few Asian rivers and coastal lagoons, and Chilika's population, counted at around 150 in recent years, is among the largest in a single lagoon anywhere. They gather near the outer channel by **Satapada**, where boatmen take tourists to watch. Their numbers were once falling, harmed by nets and motorboats. Since the new sea mouth in 2000 and stricter rules on boat traffic and gill nets, counts have recovered. The dolphins sometimes spit jets of water to herd fish, a trick they share with their cousins in the Mekong.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of India's few lagoon dolphins and a gauge of Chilika's health.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dolphin with no nose, that spits to go fishing.

spotlights.name: Saltwater crocodiles of Bhitarkanika
spotlights.spot_it: Huge crocodiles basking on mud banks between mangrove roots, tidal creeks all around.
spotlights.story_md: When the government began a crocodile conservation project in **1975**, Bhitarkanika's saltwater crocodiles were nearly gone. Eggs were collected, hatched safely at Dangmal and the young released. The annual count now puts the population around **1,800**, the largest in India. Some are very big: a male measured at about 7 m was claimed as a record in 2006, though giant sizes are hard to confirm. Bhitarkanika's mangroves, a Ramsar site since 2002, also shelter king cobras, water monitors and the turtles of Gahirmatha next door.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of India's clearest conservation comebacks.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bhitarkanika: from near zero in 1975 to about 1,800 crocodiles.

spotlights.name: Similipal's black tigers
spotlights.spot_it: A tiger whose stripes are so wide they merge into black bands across the back and head.
spotlights.story_md: They are called **pseudo-melanistic**: not all black, but with stripes widened and fused. In 2021 scientists at the National Centre for Biological Sciences, Bengaluru, traced the look to a single change in a gene called **Taqpep**. Around a third of Similipal's tigers carry it, and the variant is almost absent from tigers elsewhere. The reason is isolation: a small population cut off from other forests inbreeds, and a rare gene becomes common. The state plans a melanistic tiger safari near Baripada. Similipal also holds waterfalls such as Barehipani and Joranda and a large population of elephants.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A striking look that is also a warning about isolated, inbred wildlife.
spotlights.memory_hook: Black tigers: beautiful proof that a forest is too cut off.

sections.title: Kalinga: the war that changed an emperor
sections.intro_md:
Ancient Odisha was **Kalinga**, a coastal kingdom strong enough that the Mauryan empire had to conquer it by force. Around **261 BCE**, in the eighth year of his reign, **Ashoka** invaded. His own inscription, Rock Edict 13, counts **100,000 killed** and **150,000 deported**, and many more dead from hunger and disease. Then, unusually for a conqueror, he says he felt remorse, and turned to dhamma, a moral code of non-violence and fair rule. The battlefield is traditionally placed at **Dhauli**, on the Daya river near Bhubaneswar.

Kalinga rose again. In the 1st century BCE (dates vary) King **Kharavela** made it a regional power and left a long inscription about his reign on Udayagiri hill. Later, Buddhism flourished: the monasteries of **Ratnagiri, Lalitgiri and Udayagiri** in Jajpur district, now called the Diamond Triangle, drew monks for centuries. How historians know: inscriptions on rock, excavated cities such as **Sisupalgarh**, coins, and Chinese pilgrims' notes.

spotlights.name: Dhauli: the edicts and the elephant
spotlights.spot_it: A low rocky hill by a river, an elephant carved half out of a boulder, and a white Japanese-style dome on top.
spotlights.story_md: Here is the twist. At Dhauli, and at Jaugada in Ganjam, Ashoka's rock inscriptions **leave out Edict 13**, the one that confesses the slaughter. In its place are two special 'Kalinga edicts' addressed to local officials, telling them to rule justly, with the line **'All men are my children'**. Above the inscription, the front half of an elephant emerges from the rock, among the oldest rock-cut sculptures in India. On the hilltop stands the white **Shanti Stupa**, built in **1972** with Japanese Buddhist help.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where Ashoka's turn to non-violence is remembered, in his own words.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Kalinga itself, Ashoka skipped the confession and wrote: all men are my children.

spotlights.name: Udayagiri and the Hathigumpha inscription
spotlights.spot_it: Two sandstone hills honeycombed with small cells and verandas, the largest a two-storey courtyard with carved friezes.
spotlights.story_md: The twin hills hold about **33 rock-cut caves** made as shelters for Jain monks. The grandest, **Rani Gumpha**, has two storeys and friezes of processions, hunts and dancers. On the overhang of **Hathigumpha**, the elephant cave, King **Kharavela** had a 17-line inscription carved in Brahmi script. It is a year-by-year record of his reign: canals repaired, festivals held, wars fought, and a Jain image that a Nanda king had carried off from Kalinga, brought home. It also contains the word *Bharadhavasa*, often cited as one of the earliest written uses of the name Bharatavarsha.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the few royal autobiographies to survive from ancient India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kharavela wrote his CV on a cave roof, and India's name is in it.

spotlights.name: Ratnagiri
spotlights.spot_it: Brick monastery walls on a low hill, a doorway of intricately carved chlorite and large serene Buddha heads.
spotlights.story_md: Ratnagiri, 'hill of jewels', was a major Buddhist monastery for perhaps 800 years and a centre of Vajrayana, the tantric Buddhism that later shaped Tibet. Excavations from **1958 to 1961**, led by Debala Mitra, uncovered two monasteries, a great stupa, hundreds of votive stupas and many Buddha images. New digs by the Archaeological Survey of India in 2024 and 2025 found more, including a huge stone Buddha head and a giant carved hand, and fed fresh interest in Odisha's links with Southeast Asia. With Lalitgiri and Udayagiri nearby it forms the Diamond Triangle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that Odisha was a Buddhist hub long after Ashoka.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ratnagiri: a hill of jewels that was really a hill of monks.

sections.title: When Kalinga sailed to Bali
sections.intro_md:
For more than a thousand years, ships from the ports of Kalinga, at Tamralipti, Palur and the mouths of the Mahanadi, sailed to Sri Lanka, Burma, Java, Sumatra and Bali. They rode the winter north-east winds out and the summer monsoon back, carrying cloth, pepper, ivory and ideas. Odia sailors were called **sadhabas**, and their ships **boitas**.

The traces are scattered across Asia. In Malay and Indonesian, people from India were long called **Keling**, a word usually traced to Kalinga. Scripts and temple styles in Southeast Asia show influence from India's east coast, though historians argue over how much came from Odisha in particular.

Odisha remembers this every year at the full moon of the month of Kartika, in October or November, when people float little boats at dawn and Cuttack holds one of Asia's largest open-air fairs.

spotlights.name: Bali Jatra and Boita Bandana
spotlights.spot_it: Before sunrise, families at rivers and ponds float tiny boats of banana bark, paper or cork with lamps inside.
spotlights.story_md: The ritual is **Boita Bandana**, the worship of the boats. Women and children launch the little boats and sing 'Aa ka ma bai', a song remembering the months when sailors set off and wives waited. In Cuttack, on the banks of the Mahanadi, the **Bali Jatra**, 'voyage to Bali', grows into a fair lasting about a week, with hundreds of stalls, food, rides and cultural shows, drawing lakhs of visitors. It is one of the largest open-air trade fairs in Asia. The festival keeps alive a memory of maritime trade that ended centuries ago.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living memory of Odisha's seafaring past.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every Kartika full moon, Odisha sends a paper fleet to Bali.

sections.title: Temple city and the Kalinga style
sections.intro_md:
Odisha has its own school of temple building, called the **Kalinga style**. Its temples have two main parts. The **deula** or **rekha deula** is a tall sanctuary tower with a curving outline that bends inward near the top, capped by a ribbed stone disc called an **amalaka**. In front stands the **jagamohana** or **pidha deula**, a porch whose roof is a stepped pyramid of flat tiers. Bigger temples add a dance hall and an offering hall in a line.

You can watch the style grow in one city. Bhubaneswar's early temples, such as **Parasurameswara** (about 7th century), are small and squat. **Mukteswar** (10th century) is compact and perfect. **Lingaraj** (11th century) is the full statement. The Jagannath temple at Puri and Konark follow. The builders worked largely without mortar, holding blocks in place with weight, balance and iron clamps.

Odisha also has two rare **yogini temples**, circular and open to the sky, made for tantric worship.

visual.title: Two parts of a Kalinga temple

spotlights.name: Lingaraj Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A soaring red-brown sandstone tower, its curve bending in at the top, rising above a walled compound packed with smaller shrines.
spotlights.story_md: Lingaraj's main tower is about **55 m** tall, and the compound holds more than a hundred smaller shrines. The deity is unusual: a lingam worshipped as **Harihara**, a combined form of Shiva and Vishnu, which is why both Shaiva and Vaishnava rites are performed here. The temple is still fully active, with its own kitchens and hereditary priests. Non-Hindus are not allowed inside; a raised viewing platform beside the north wall lets visitors see over the wall. During Ashokashtami the deity travels by chariot, a smaller cousin of Puri's Rath Yatra.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most complete statement of the Kalinga temple style.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lingaraj: 55 m of stone, Shiva and Vishnu sharing one god.

spotlights.name: Mukteswar Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A small, jewel-like temple fronted by a free-standing arched gateway, a torana, carved with reclining women.
spotlights.story_md: At only about 10 m tall, Mukteswar is tiny next to Lingaraj, yet architectural historians call it the gem of Odisha temple architecture. It is the first in the region with a decorated **torana**, a stone arch rising from two pillars like a frozen garland. Its surfaces show monkeys acting out the Panchatantra fables, ascetics teaching, and lion heads with beaded tassels. It marks the shift from the early to the mature Kalinga style. Every January the **Mukteswar Dance Festival** sets Odissi performances against its floodlit walls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that perfect proportion, not size, made Kalinga temples great.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mukteswar: Odisha's smallest masterpiece, with a stone garland at the gate.

spotlights.name: Chausath Yogini Temple, Hirapur
spotlights.spot_it: A small, round, roofless stone enclosure with 64 dark goddess figures in niches around the inside wall.
spotlights.story_md: The temple is a circle about 7.6 m across, open to the sky because yoginis were believed to fly. Inside, **64 yoginis** carved in black chlorite stand in niches, each a fierce or graceful goddess on her own animal or object. Tradition credits Queen **Hiradevi** of the Bhauma-Kara dynasty. The yoginis were part of tantric practices that later became secret and then faded. Only a handful of such temples survive in India, two of them in Odisha, at Hirapur and Ranipur-Jharial. It lay largely forgotten until rediscovered in the 1950s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It preserves a rare form of goddess worship that almost vanished.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hirapur: a temple with no roof, so the goddesses can fly.

sections.title: Jagannath: the god who leaves home
sections.intro_md:
If Odisha has one centre, it is **Jagannath**, 'lord of the universe', in his temple at **Puri**. The present temple was begun by **Anantavarman Chodaganga** of the Eastern Ganga dynasty in the 12th century; its tower is about 65 m tall, and a flag on top is changed every evening by a priest who climbs it by hand.

Jagannath is worshipped with his elder brother **Balabhadra** and sister **Subhadra**. They are carved from wood, not stone, with huge round eyes and no full hands or feet. The worship mixes Vaishnava devotion with very old local and tribal elements: some of the god's closest servants, the **daitapatis**, are believed to descend from a tribal chief, Viswavasu, who first worshipped the deity in the forest.

The temple runs like a small city, with about 36 categories of hereditary servitors. And unlike most temple gods, Jagannath leaves home: once a year he rides out in a chariot through the street to meet his devotees, including those not allowed inside.

spotlights.name: Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra
spotlights.spot_it: Three wooden deities in a row: black Jagannath with huge round eyes, white Balabhadra, and smaller yellow Subhadra.
spotlights.story_md: The forms are like nothing else in Hindu art: stumps for arms, faces that are mostly eyes and a wide smile. A legend explains it. King **Indradyumna** hired an old carpenter who agreed to carve the deities only if no one opened the door for 21 days. The anxious queen opened it early, the carpenter vanished, and the gods remained unfinished. Scholars see older roots: the shapes resemble tribal wooden post-deities of central and eastern India. The colours matter too. The icons appear all over Odisha, on buses, shop shutters and wedding cards.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Jagannath ties Odisha's Hindu, tribal and regional identities together.
spotlights.memory_hook: The god with no hands, worshipped by a state that will not let him go.

spotlights.name: Rath Yatra
spotlights.when: Ashadha month, June or July; 16 July in 2026
spotlights.spot_it: Three towering wooden chariots with striped canopies, hauled by thick ropes through a sea of people on a wide road.
spotlights.story_md: Each year three new chariots are built from fresh timber by hereditary carpenters: **Nandighosa** for Jagannath, 16 wheels and about 13.5 m tall; **Taladhwaja** for Balabhadra, 14 wheels; and **Darpadalana** for Subhadra, 12 wheels. Before they roll, the **Gajapati king of Puri** sweeps the chariot floors with a gold-handled broom, a ritual called **Chhera Pahanra**, showing that the king is the god's servant. Devotees pull the chariots about 3 km along the Bada Danda to the **Gundicha Temple**, where the deities stay a week. The English word **juggernaut** comes from this festival.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the largest religious gatherings in India, and one of the oldest chariot festivals.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king with a golden broom, and a god who needs a million hands to go out.

spotlights.name: Nabakalebara: the new body
spotlights.spot_it: Freshly carved wooden deities replacing the old ones; a felled neem log carried to Puri in procession.
spotlights.story_md: Because the deities are wood, they must be renewed. In years with an extra month of Ashadha, which happens every 8, 12 or 19 years, the temple holds **Nabakalebara**, 'new body'. Search parties of daitapatis go out to find **daru**, sacred neem trees that meet a list of signs: near a river and a cremation ground, with a snake's home nearby, and marks like a conch or wheel on the bark. New images are carved in secret. At midnight, blindfolded servitors move a mysterious *brahma padartha*, the life-substance, from old to new. The old images are buried. The 2015 festival drew more than three million people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare ritual of a god who is replaced and buried.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every dozen years or so, Jagannath dies and is reborn from a neem tree.

spotlights.name: The temple kitchen and Mahaprasad
spotlights.spot_it: Food in unglazed clay pots, eaten from leaf plates, sold in the temple's Ananda Bazaar.
spotlights.story_md: Puri's temple kitchen is often called one of the largest in the world. Hundreds of hereditary cooks, the suaras, work at hundreds of wood-fired clay hearths, with figures given from about 240 to more than 750. Food is cooked in new earthen pots stacked one on another, and temple tradition holds that the top pot cooks first. After it is offered to Jagannath it becomes **Mahaprasad** and is sold in the **Ananda Bazaar** market inside the walls. Here, by tradition, people of all castes eat together from the same pots, an exception in a society that long policed who could eat with whom. The daily menu of **56 items** is called Chhappan Bhoga.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Mahaprasad breaks caste rules in the heart of an orthodox temple.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Puri's Ananda Bazaar, the god's leftovers make everyone equal.

sections.title: How Odisha became Odisha
sections.intro_md:
At its height in the 15th century, the **Gajapati** empire of **Kapilendra Deva**, founded in **1434**, stretched from the Ganga in Bengal to the Kaveri in Tamil Nadu. It did not last. After **Mukunda Deva**, the last independent king, died in **1568**, Odisha passed to the Afghans of Bengal, then the Mughals, then the Marathas from 1751, and finally the British East India Company in **1803**.

British rule split the Odia-speaking people among the Bengal, Madras and Central Provinces presidencies, and Odia faced pressure to be replaced by Bengali in schools. Disaster sharpened the sense of neglect. Then came a long campaign, led by lawyers, writers and princes, to bring all Odia speakers under one administration.

It worked. On **1 April 1936** Orissa became a separate province, the first in India created on the basis of language, 16 years before Andhra's movement made the idea national. The princely states, including Mayurbhanj, merged by 1949.

spotlights.name: The Paika rebellion
spotlights.spot_it: The name Paika recalls foot soldiers with swords and shields; a memorial stands in Khurda.
spotlights.story_md: The **paikas** were a hereditary peasant militia who held rent-free land in return for military service to the king of Khurda. After the British took Odisha in 1803 they lost their land, the salt trade fell under a company monopoly, and taxes had to be paid in silver. In **1817**, led by **Bakshi Jagabandhu**, the former military commander of Khurda, the paikas rose up, attacked British posts and briefly took Puri. The revolt was crushed by 1818, though Jagabandhu stayed free until 1825. In 2017 the bicentenary was marked nationally, and some Odisha leaders call it India's first war of independence, a claim historians debate.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Odisha's founding story of resistance to company rule.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty years before 1857, Odisha's soldiers had already risen.

spotlights.name: Madhusudan Das
spotlights.spot_it: A stern bearded lawyer in a high collar, known in Odisha as Utkal Gourav, the pride of Utkal.
spotlights.story_md: Madhusudan Das was the first Odia to earn a university degree and the first Odia lawyer. In **1903** he founded the **Utkal Sammilani**, the Utkal Union Conference, which campaigned for decades to unite Odia-speaking areas. He was also a businessman: his **Utkal Tannery** made shoes and leather goods, and he promoted Odia crafts such as silver filigree. He served as a minister in Bihar and Orissa province. He died in 1934, two years before the province he worked for was born. His birthday, 28 April, is marked as Lawyers' Day in Odisha.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned a cultural grievance into a political movement that succeeded.
spotlights.memory_hook: Madhusudan Das fought 30 years for Odisha and missed it by two.

sections.title: Round letters and palm leaves
sections.intro_md:
Odia is an Indo-Aryan language spoken by about 3.5 to 4 crore people, mostly in Odisha. In **2014** it became India's sixth **classical language**, the first Indo-Aryan language after Sanskrit to get the status, recognising more than a thousand years of literature. The earliest Odia words appear in inscriptions from around the 10th century.

The medieval poet **Sarala Das** wrote an Odia Mahabharata in the 15th century, retelling the epic with local places and characters. In the 16th century the **Panchasakha**, five poet-saints, put religious texts into everyday Odia so ordinary people could read them. **Jayadeva's** Sanskrit Gita Govinda, composed in Odisha in the 12th century, became part of Jagannath's daily worship and the backbone of Odissi dance.

Modern Odia prose was born in the 1890s, and among its first great works is a satire about a stolen plot of land.

spotlights.name: The Odia script
spotlights.when: Script developed by about the 14th century
spotlights.spot_it: Letters made mostly of curves, many topped by a rounded hood rather than a straight line.
spotlights.story_md: Odia letters are round for a practical reason. Writers for centuries scratched text onto **dried palm leaves** with an iron stylus, then rubbed in soot to make it visible. Long straight horizontal strokes, like the headline across Hindi letters, would split the leaf along its grain. So scribes curved them. The result is one of India's most recognisable scripts, descended from Brahmi through the eastern Siddham family and related to Bengali. Odia was added to Unicode in 1991.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a script shaped by its writing material.
spotlights.memory_hook: Odia letters are round because straight lines would split the leaf.

spotlights.name: Fakir Mohan Senapati
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded writer in an old photograph, honoured by a university in Balasore that carries his name.
spotlights.story_md: Fakir Mohan Senapati grew up poor in Balasore and taught himself. When Bengali scholars claimed Odia was only a dialect of Bengali, he fought back with books. His novel **Chha Mana Atha Guntha**, 'Six Acres and a Third', serialised from 1897 and published in 1902, follows a greedy landlord who schemes to steal a weaver couple's small plot. It is funny, cruel and told by a sarcastic narrator who pretends to praise the villain. Critics count it among the first Indian novels about the exploitation of ordinary peasants. An English translation came out in 2005.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed Odia could carry a modern novel.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six acres and a third: the land grab that made Odia literature modern.

sections.title: Odissi, Gotipua and Chhau
sections.intro_md:
Odisha's dance runs from temple to village square. **Odissi**, one of India's classical dances, is the most famous. Its poses are carved on the walls of Konark and on the 2,000-year-old Rani Gumpha cave at Udayagiri, which is why dancers say their art is written in stone.

For centuries the dance was kept by **maharis**, women dedicated to Jagannath's temple who danced in the inner rituals, and by **gotipuas**, boys dressed as girls who danced in public. Under British rule and social reform, the mahari tradition declined. In the late 1940s and 1950s a group of gurus, dancers and scholars, the **Jayantika** circle, pieced Odissi back together from these lineages, temple sculpture and old texts on dance. The modern form is their reconstruction, a fact dancers openly debate.

In the north, **Chhau** is a martial dance from Mayurbhanj; in the west, **Sambalpuri** folk dances move to the beat of the dhol and nishan drums.

spotlights.name: Odissi
spotlights.when: Reconstructed in the 1950s from older traditions
spotlights.spot_it: A dancer bent into three curves, head, torso and hips, then dropping into a deep square stance with knees out.
spotlights.story_md: Two positions define it. **Tribhangi**, 'three bends', tilts head, chest and hips in opposite directions, the S-curve of temple sculpture. **Chauka**, 'square', is a low, wide stance said to represent Jagannath himself. A typical recital opens with **mangalacharan**, an invocation, moves through **pallavi**, pure dance that blossoms with the music, and **abhinaya**, acted poetry usually from the Gita Govinda, and ends in **moksha**, release. Dancers wear silver jewellery from Cuttack, a crown of pith called the tahia, and a sari of Sambalpuri or Bomkai silk.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how Odisha shows itself to the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three bends and a square: the body language of Odisha's temples.

spotlights.name: Kelucharan Mohapatra
spotlights.spot_it: A slight older man in dhoti, eyes and hands doing most of the dancing.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **Raghurajpur**, the village of painters, Kelucharan Mohapatra danced as a **gotipua** boy, played the pakhawaj drum in a theatre troupe and learned pattachitra painting. From these pieces he became the most influential guru in modern Odissi, part of the group that rebuilt the style in the 1950s and choreographer of many of its classic pieces. His students include **Sanjukta Panigrahi**, the first Odia woman to take up Odissi as a career, and **Protima Gauri Bedi**, who founded the dance village Nrityagram near Bengaluru in 1990. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 2000.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One man carried a village tradition onto the world stage.
spotlights.memory_hook: A painter's son from Raghurajpur taught the world to dance Odissi.

spotlights.name: Gotipua
spotlights.spot_it: Young boys in saris and heavy make-up, hair in a bun with flowers, bending backward into acrobatic human sculptures.
spotlights.story_md: **Gotipua** means 'single boy'. The tradition is said to have started around the 16th century, when the maharis' dance was restricted and devout followers trained boys, dressed as girls, to dance for Jagannath in public. Boys begin as young as six and stop when their bodies change in their teens. The dance mixes Odissi steps with **bandha nritya**, acrobatics in which boys fold into knots or form pyramids, often to songs about Radha and Krishna. Gurukuls in Raghurajpur still train them, though numbers have fallen.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It kept Odissi alive in public when the temple tradition faded.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gotipua: boys who dance as girls until their voices break.

spotlights.name: Mayurbhanj Chhau
spotlights.spot_it: Bare-faced male dancers in a vigorous martial crouch, leaping and stamping to loud drums and shehnai.
spotlights.story_md: Chhau is danced in three styles across eastern India: Seraikela in Jharkhand, Purulia in West Bengal and Mayurbhanj in Odisha. UNESCO inscribed all three together on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in **2010**. The Mayurbhanj form is the only one danced **without masks**, so the face stays still while the body tells the story, often episodes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. Its moves come from mock combat and from animal and bird movements. It is performed most of all during the spring **Chaitra Parva** in Baripada, once under the patronage of the Mayurbhanj royal family.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is martial art turned into theatre, and an Odia entry on the UNESCO list.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mayurbhanj Chhau: the one without masks.

sections.title: Painters, weavers and silversmiths
sections.intro_md:
Odisha's crafts grew around the Jagannath temple, which needed paintings, banners, umbrellas, cloth and ornaments for its endless rituals, and around royal courts and village markets. Many crafts are made by whole villages that specialise: painters in **Raghurajpur**, appliqué workers in **Pipili**, weavers in **Nuapatna**, Sonepur and Bargarh, and silversmiths in **Cuttack**.

Several now carry **Geographical Indication** tags, which protect a name the way Champagne is protected in France: Odisha pattachitra, Pipili appliqué, Sambalpuri bandha sarees, Kotpad handloom, Konark stone carving and, since 2024, Cuttack's silver filigree.

The newest Odia craft is the oldest material of all: sand. One Puri artist has turned beach sculptures into a global form.

spotlights.name: Pattachitra and Raghurajpur
spotlights.when: Living tradition; Raghurajpur heritage village since 2000
spotlights.spot_it: Bold outlines, flat bright colours and a decorated border, gods and animals filling every inch of a cloth painting.
spotlights.story_md: **Patta** means cloth, **chitra** picture. Painters coat cotton with a paste of tamarind seed and chalk, polish it with a stone and paint with natural colours: white from conch shells, black from lamp soot, red from **hingula** (cinnabar) and yellow from haritala. Brushes are made from mouse or squirrel hair. The most sacred are the **anasara patti**, paintings worshipped in place of Jagannath during the two weeks each year when the deities are said to be ill after their ritual bath. In **Raghurajpur**, a village of little more than a hundred households near Puri, almost every house is a studio, with painted walls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a temple art that became one of India's best-known folk paintings.
spotlights.memory_hook: When Jagannath falls ill, a painting takes his place.

spotlights.name: Sambalpuri ikat (bandha)
spotlights.spot_it: A saree whose motifs have soft, slightly blurred edges, with conch, wheel and flower patterns.
spotlights.story_md: In **bandha** ikat, the pattern is dyed into the threads before weaving. Weavers tie bundles of yarn tightly, dye them, untie, retie and dye again, so each thread carries its colours in exactly the right places. When woven, the design appears, with the slight feathery blur that marks real ikat. Classic motifs are **shankha** (conch), **chakra** (wheel) and **phula** (flower). Indira Gandhi wore Sambalpuri sarees often, which made them nationally famous. In **Nuapatna**, weavers make **Khandua** silk with lines of the Gita Govinda woven in, for Jagannath himself.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of India's most complex weaves, and an everyday Odia pride.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sambalpuri: the pattern is in the thread before the cloth exists.

spotlights.name: Pipili appliqué
spotlights.spot_it: Shops hung with bright red, yellow and black cloth umbrellas, lanterns and bags, decorated with cut-out animals, flowers and tiny mirrors.
spotlights.story_md: In **Pipili**, a highway town between Bhubaneswar and Puri, tailors cut shapes of elephants, parrots, suns and flowers from coloured cloth and stitch them onto a base. The craft began as temple work: the canopies, umbrellas and banners for Jagannath's chariots are still made by Pipili families. Today the same workshops make garden umbrellas, wall hangings and cushion covers for tourists, and the craft holds a GI tag. The colours follow the temple: red, yellow, black, white and green, the palette of the three deities.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a temple craft became a market craft.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pipili: the town that dresses Jagannath's chariots.

spotlights.name: Cuttack silver filigree (tarakasi)
spotlights.spot_it: Lace-like silver, made of fine twisted wire coiled into flowers and scrolls.
spotlights.story_md: **Tara** means wire and **kasi** design. Smiths draw silver into hair-fine wire, twist it, and solder it into frames like silver lace. The craft may have reached Cuttack through trade with Southeast Asia or Persia centuries ago; by the 19th century Cuttack was India's filigree capital. Odissi dancers wear its jewellery, and at Durga Puja whole pandal backdrops, called **chandi medha**, are built of silver filigree. Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi received its Geographical Indication tag in 2024. Cheaper machine-made imitations are the craft's biggest threat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Cuttack's signature and a rare surviving filigree centre.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cuttack spins silver into lace.

sections.title: Sixty-two peoples
sections.intro_md:
Odisha lists **62 Scheduled Tribes**, more than any other state, and **13** of them are Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups, the smallest and most at risk, also the most of any state. Together they are about **22.8%** of the population, around 96 lakh people in 2011. The largest are the **Khond (Kondh)**, Gond, **Santal**, Saora and Munda.

They speak languages from three families: Austroasiatic (Santali, Ho, Sora, Bonda's Remo), Dravidian (Kui, Kuvi, Gondi) and Indo-Aryan. Most live in the hilly south and west and the northern plateau, the same land that holds the minerals. That overlap is the central conflict of modern Odisha: forests and sacred hills on one side, iron, bauxite and coal under them.

Tribal heritage is also everywhere in mainstream Odisha: in the forms of Jagannath, in festival dances, and since 2022 in the office of India's President, held by a Santal woman from Mayurbhanj.

spotlights.name: The Dongria Kondh and Niyamgiri
spotlights.spot_it: Women with three gold rings in the nose and hair pinned with clips; men in embroidered shawls; green ridges behind.
spotlights.story_md: The **Dongria Kondh**, roughly 8,000 to 10,000 people, live on the **Niyamgiri** hills and worship the mountain as **Niyam Raja**, the god of law. Under the hills lies bauxite. When Vedanta built an alumina refinery at Lanjigarh and planned to mine the summit, the Dongria protested for years. In **April 2013** the Supreme Court ruled that local village councils must decide. That summer all **12 gram sabhas** chosen voted no, and the mining plan was rejected. Their embroidered **kapdaganda** shawls, green, red and yellow on white, are now famous.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was a landmark for the right of tribal villages to refuse mining.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve villages said no to a mining giant, and the mountain god won.

spotlights.name: The Bonda
spotlights.spot_it: Women with shaved heads under beaded caps, wrapped in many strands of colourful beads and brass neck rings, wearing a short woven skirt.
spotlights.story_md: The **Bonda**, who call themselves **Remo**, live in the remote hills of Malkangiri near the Andhra border and speak an Austroasiatic language. They are among the most isolated communities in India, and their women's dress, layers of bead necklaces covering the chest and a short ringa skirt, has made them the most photographed. That attention has a cost: weekly markets at Onukudelli became tourist sights, and the state now restricts photography and visits. Literacy has been low, though more Bonda children now attend residential schools.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They show how fragile small communities are when they become a spectacle.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Bonda: beads as clothing, and a right not to be photographed.

spotlights.name: Saura idital wall paintings
spotlights.spot_it: White stick figures of people, horses, elephants and trees arranged inside a square frame on a red-ochre mud wall.
spotlights.story_md: The **Lanjia Saura** paint **idital** on house walls, mostly with white rice paste on ochre. They are not decoration. A shaman, often a woman, called the **kudan**, tells the painter what the spirits or ancestors want, and the painting is made as an offering, crowded with figures of people, animals, sun, moon and everyday tools. Their language, Sora, is Austroasiatic, and in **1936** a Saura man, **Mangei Gomango**, created a new script for it, **Sorang Sompeng**. Today the style is printed on cushion covers and city walls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a sacred tribal art now borrowed by design shops.
spotlights.memory_hook: Saura idital: a letter to the ancestors, painted on the wall.

sections.title: Rice, water and cheese
sections.intro_md:
Odia food is rice food, gentle on spice and built on vegetables, lentils, fish and a five-spice mix called **pancha phutana**: cumin, mustard, fennel, fenugreek and nigella. Mustard paste and mustard oil give fish and vegetable curries their bite. Meals at home are often no onion, no garlic on ritual days, a habit linked to the temple kitchen.

The temple shapes much of it. The 56 dishes of the Jagannath Mahaprasad include **dalma**, rice, **kanika** (sweet rice), **khechudi** and many sweets; Odia cooks say the temple is the cuisine's textbook.

The other influence is heat. A dish of rice soaked overnight in water is the summer staple of millions. And Odisha is a land of **chhena**, fresh cheese, which it turns into some of India's most argued-over sweets.

spotlights.name: Pakhala
spotlights.when: Everyday, especially summer; Pakhala Dibasa on 20 March
spotlights.spot_it: A bowl of rice sitting in water, with fried fish, a green chilli, onion and a dry vegetable on the side.
spotlights.story_md: **Pakhala** is cooked rice soaked in water, sometimes left to ferment lightly overnight, sometimes flavoured with curd, cumin and curry leaves. It cools the body in a 45°C summer and keeps rice from spoiling without a fridge. It is eaten with fried fish, **badi chura** (crushed sun-dried lentil dumplings), saga (greens), potatoes or mashed brinjal. Since the 2010s Odias have celebrated **Pakhala Dibasa** on **20 March**, a social-media holiday that stuck. The temple also offers pakhala to Jagannath in summer.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case of food designed by climate.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pakhala: Odisha's air conditioning, served in a bowl.

spotlights.name: Rasagola
spotlights.spot_it: Soft white or cream cheese balls in light syrup; the Pahala kind is often slightly browned.
spotlights.story_md: The sweet started a war of words. Odisha says the **rasagola** has been offered at Puri for centuries: on **Niladri Bije**, the day Jagannath returns from Rath Yatra, he offers rasagola to his wife **Lakshmi**, who is angry at being left behind. West Bengal credits the Kolkata confectioner **Nobin Chandra Das** with the spongy rosogolla in 1868. Bengal won a GI tag for 'Banglar Rasogolla' in **2017**; Odisha won one for 'Odisha Rasagola' in **2019**. Both can claim a version; neither tag decides who was first. Odisha marks Rasagola Dibasa on Niladri Bije.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how food becomes identity and law.
spotlights.memory_hook: Jagannath pays his wife a rasagola to be let back in the house.

spotlights.name: Dalma
spotlights.spot_it: A thick yellow lentil stew full of chunks of vegetables, topped with a tempering of cumin and red chilli.
spotlights.story_md: **Dalma** is toor or moong dal cooked with chunks of raw papaya, pumpkin, brinjal, potato, plantain and yam, then tempered with **pancha phutana** and roasted cumin-chilli powder. The temple version uses no onion, garlic, tomato or chilli, because those were unknown or forbidden in the old ritual kitchen. It is Odisha's comfort food and its public food: since **2015**, the state's **Aahaar** centres have served a meal of rice and dalma for ₹5. A chain of restaurants in Bhubaneswar is even called Dalma.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the everyday dish that best shows Odia cooking's balance.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dalma: one pot, all the vegetables, five rupees.

sections.title: A year of festivals
sections.intro_md:
Odias joke that the state has **thirteen festivals in twelve months** (baro masa tera parba). Many follow Jagannath's calendar: his bath at **Snana Purnima**, two weeks of seclusion, then Rath Yatra. Others follow the farm: **Nuakhai** for the new rice in the west, **Raja** for the earth's rest before sowing.

The autumn brings **Durga Puja**, nowhere grander in Odisha than in Cuttack, and Kartika month brings the dawn boats of Boita Bandana and the Bali Jatra fair. Winter brings **Dhanu Jatra** in Bargarh, where a whole town becomes a stage. Spring brings Chaitra Parva and Chhau in Mayurbhanj, and the hot season ends with **Chandan Yatra**, when Jagannath's representatives are rowed on the temple tank to cool off.

The ring below places the big ones by month.

data.name: Chaitra Parva and Chhau; Odia New Year

spotlights.name: Raja Parba
spotlights.when: Mid-June, three days around Mithuna Sankranti
spotlights.spot_it: Young women in new saris laughing on rope swings hung from trees, plates of poda pitha and paan nearby.
spotlights.story_md: **Raja** celebrates the earth as a woman. For three days in mid-June, as the monsoon arrives, the earth goddess **Bhudevi** is believed to be menstruating, and so she rests. No ploughing, sowing or digging. Women and girls also rest from housework, wear new clothes, play cards and games, and swing on decorated **doli** swings while singing Raja songs. Homes make **poda pitha**, a baked rice cake. On the fourth day the earth is given a ritual bath. It is a festival that treats menstruation as fertility, not impurity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare festival celebrating menstruation openly.
spotlights.memory_hook: For three days in June, the earth and its women take a holiday.

spotlights.name: Dhanu Jatra
spotlights.spot_it: A costumed king Kansa on an elephant parading through a real town, crowds following, stages scattered across the streets.
spotlights.story_md: For 11 days the town of **Bargarh** becomes Mathura and the river Jira becomes the Yamuna. A village across the river becomes Gopapura, Krishna's childhood home. The story of Krishna and his evil uncle Kansa is acted across the whole town, and the actor playing **King Kansa** truly rules it: he can summon officials, fine passers-by and scold ministers, all in character. The festival began in 1947 to 1948, celebrating independence as the end of a tyrant. It is often called the world's largest open-air theatre.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns a town into a stage and power into play.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Bargarh each winter, a demon king can fine a minister.

spotlights.name: Nuakhai
spotlights.spot_it: Families in new clothes, a plate of new rice offered first to the goddess, then shared; elders blessing the young.
spotlights.story_md: **Nua** means new, **khai** means food. The first rice of the season is offered to the goddess, in Sambalpur to **Samaleswari**, at an hour fixed by priests, and then the whole family eats together. The young touch elders' feet and say **Nuakhai juhar**. People who have moved away try to come home, much as for a harvest festival elsewhere. Sambalpuri dances and songs fill the evening. It is the biggest festival of western Odisha and a marker of its distinct identity, culture and Sambalpuri language.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It anchors western Odisha's identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nuakhai: the year's new rice, eaten first by a goddess.

sections.title: From ten thousand dead to almost none
sections.intro_md:
The Bay of Bengal makes more severe cyclones than the Arabian Sea, and Odisha's low coast lies straight in their path. Storm surges can push the sea kilometres inland.

On **29 October 1999** a super cyclone hit near **Paradip** with winds around 260 km/h and a surge of 5 to 6 m. Close to **10,000 people** died, most in Jagatsinghpur district. Within weeks Odisha set up India's first state disaster management authority, **OSDMA**, years before a national law required one.

What followed was a quiet revolution: hundreds of raised **multipurpose cyclone shelters**, volunteers trained in each village, warnings in plain Odia, and an approach that counted every person moved. When **Phailin**, almost as strong, hit in **2013**, about a million people were evacuated and deaths fell to a few dozen. In **2019** Odisha moved over a million people ahead of **Fani**. The United Nations praised it as a model. The goal Odisha now announces before each storm is **zero casualties**.

visual.title: Deaths in Odisha from three severe cyclones

spotlights.name: The 1999 super cyclone
spotlights.spot_it: Satellite image of a huge, tight spiral with a clear eye over the bay just off the coast.
spotlights.story_md: The storm sat over the coast for more than a day and a half, which made it deadlier. The surge swept over **Ersama** block in Jagatsinghpur, where entire villages vanished; survivors spent days on rooftops and trees with bodies around them. Official deaths were about **9,900**, along with lakhs of cattle, and well over a crore people were affected. Communications broke down so completely that the scale was not known in Bhubaneswar for days. A separate severe cyclone had struck southern Odisha less than two weeks earlier. The disaster became Odisha's turning point in disaster planning.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is why Odisha now leads India in cyclone response.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ersama, 1999: the storm that taught a state to evacuate.

spotlights.name: Phailin and Fani: the turnaround
spotlights.spot_it: Raised concrete buildings on pillars in coastal villages, painted with a cyclone shelter sign, crowded during a storm.
spotlights.story_md: **Phailin** made landfall near Gopalpur on **12 October 2013**. Odisha and Andhra moved about a million people, and deaths stayed in the dozens. **Fani** struck near Puri on **3 May 2019** with winds near 175 km/h, a rare summer cyclone of that strength. Odisha evacuated more than **1.2 million people** in about a day, using shelters, schools and texts. Deaths in Odisha were reported at **64**, against close to 10,000 in 1999. The UN disaster agency singled out Odisha's work. The damage to power lines and houses was still huge; saving lives, not property, is what Odisha learned to do.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the world's clearest examples of disaster preparation saving lives.
spotlights.memory_hook: From 10,000 dead in 1999 to 64 in 2019: same coast, better plan.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Odisha's modern story is told through a few lives. A pilot who flew into a war zone to rescue another country's leaders, then ran Odisha. His son, who ran it for 24 years. A tribal woman from Mayurbhanj who became President of India. And a state government that decided Indian hockey needed a sponsor, and became one.

Others deserve a line. **Gopabandhu Das** (1877 to 1928), called Utkalmani, founded the Satyabadi school and the newspaper *The Samaja*. **Ramadevi Choudhury** led women in the freedom movement. **Nandini Satpathy** was Odisha's first woman chief minister. **Sitakant Mahapatra** and **Pratibha Ray** won the Jnanpith Award. The sprinter **Dutee Chand**, from a weaver's family in Jajpur, won Asian Games silver medals in 2018 and in 2019 became the first openly gay Indian athlete to speak publicly.

spotlights.name: Biju Patnaik
spotlights.spot_it: A broad-shouldered man in an aviator's jacket in early photos; later a thick-set politician in white.
spotlights.story_md: **Biju Patnaik** was a pilot before he was a politician. In **1947**, at Nehru's request, he flew a Dakota into Dutch-blockaded Java and brought out Indonesian leaders, including Prime Minister **Sutan Sjahrir**, to India. Indonesia later made him an honorary citizen and gave him one of its highest awards, a rare honour for a foreigner. He founded **Kalinga Airlines**, and in 1952 funded UNESCO's **Kalinga Prize** for popularising science. He was chief minister in 1961 to 1963 and 1990 to 1995. A popular story says he named Sukarno's daughter Megawati; it is often repeated, not proven.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is Odisha's larger-than-life modern hero.
spotlights.memory_hook: Biju Patnaik: chief minister of Odisha, honorary citizen of Indonesia.

spotlights.name: Naveen Patnaik
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, quiet man in a white kurta, rarely seen speaking long speeches.
spotlights.story_md: Biju's younger son lived as a writer in Delhi and abroad, and spoke little Odia, when he entered politics after his father's death in 1997. He founded the **Biju Janata Dal** and became chief minister on **5 March 2000**. He held the job until **June 2024**, more than 24 years, the second-longest unbroken term of any Indian chief minister. His years brought the cyclone revolution, cheap rice, the hockey sponsorship and steady growth, along with critics who said power had become too centred on a few officials. In 2024 his party lost to the BJP.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He defined Odisha for a generation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Naveen: 24 years in charge, in a language he barely spoke at first.

spotlights.name: Droupadi Murmu
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in a plain white or light handloom saree, hair parted in the middle, a gentle formal smile.
spotlights.story_md: Droupadi Murmu was born in **1958** into a **Santal** family in Uparbeda village, Mayurbhanj. She worked as a teacher and a government clerk, began in local politics in Rairangpur, became an Odisha MLA and minister, and was Governor of Jharkhand from 2015 to 2021. On **25 July 2022** she became India's **15th President**: the first from a Scheduled Tribe, the second woman, and the first born after independence. She has spoken openly about personal tragedies, including losing her husband and two sons, and about finding peace in meditation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is the most visible symbol of tribal India in national life.
spotlights.memory_hook: From a Mayurbhanj village school to Rashtrapati Bhavan.

spotlights.name: Odisha and Indian hockey
spotlights.spot_it: A blue pitch in a huge steel-roofed stadium; national team jerseys carrying the word Odisha.
spotlights.story_md: When the Sahara group stopped sponsoring Indian hockey in **2018**, the Odisha government stepped in to sponsor the men's and women's national teams, a first for an Indian state. It hosted the men's World Cup in **2018** and again in **2023**, building the **Birsa Munda stadium** in Rourkela with about **20,000 seats**, described as India's largest hockey stadium. Odisha's Sundargarh district is a hockey nursery: **Dilip Tirkey**, Lazarus Barla and **Amit Rohidas** come from there. India's men won Olympic bronze in Tokyo and Paris with the state's name on their kit.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a state government can revive a national sport.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's hockey jerseys say Odisha.

sections.title: How Odisha earns
sections.intro_md:
Odisha was long one of India's poorest states. In the 1990s close to half of its people lived below the poverty line. It has climbed steadily since: by the 2020s it was among India's faster-growing large states, and in **January 2025** it topped NITI Aayog's **Fiscal Health Index**, thanks to low debt and steady spending. The **2026-27** budget put its economy at about **₹11.07 lakh crore**.

The engine is minerals and metal. Odisha has most of India's **chromite**, about a third of its **bauxite** reserves by Wikipedia's count (other estimates put it near half), about a quarter of its **iron ore** and a fifth of its **coal**. Around them stand steel plants at Rourkela, Kalinganagar and Angul, aluminium at Damanjodi and Angul, and a big port at Paradip.

The costs sit in the same districts: displacement, polluted rivers such as the Brahmani near Sukinda's chromite mines, and the Niyamgiri fight. Farming still employs the most people, and seasonal migration to Gujarat and Kerala remains common.

spotlights.name: Rourkela Steel Plant
spotlights.spot_it: Blast furnaces and chimneys in a forested valley, a planned township beside them.
spotlights.story_md: Rourkela was **India's first public-sector integrated steel plant**, built in the 1950s with West German firms and engineers, while Bhilai was built with Soviet help and Durgapur with British. A tribal and forest area was turned into a planned steel city in a few years, and thousands of local families were displaced. Today it is run by **SAIL**. Rourkela's German link left traces: German engineers' children played in its townships, and the city later took up hockey with passion. Kalinganagar, further east, now holds Tata Steel's large plant.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It began Odisha's identity as a steel state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rourkela: a German-built steel city in a tribal forest.

spotlights.name: Paradip Port
spotlights.spot_it: Huge piles of coal and iron ore, cranes and long conveyor belts beside ships at a breakwater at the river mouth.
spotlights.story_md: Paradip was pushed by **Biju Patnaik**, who started building it in the early 1960s even before Delhi fully agreed. It became a major port in **1966**. It handles coal, iron ore, crude oil and fertiliser, and has an oil refinery next door. In **2023-24** it handled about **145 million tonnes** of cargo, the most of any Indian major port that year. It was the landfall point of the 1999 super cyclone and has since been rebuilt with stronger defences.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Odisha's door to the world economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paradip: Biju's port, now India's busiest major port by cargo.

sections.title: Myths, legends and arguments
sections.intro_md:
Odisha is full of stories that tour guides repeat as facts. Some are lovely legends, some are colonial exaggerations, and some are real arguments between states. Here are two worth knowing, sorted honestly, plus the rasagola argument covered in the food section.

The rule of thumb: a story told about a temple is part of its heritage and worth knowing. A story repeated as history needs a source, and many of the most famous ones do not have one. Others to treat carefully: that Puri's temple flag always flies against the wind (it follows the wind like any flag), that no bird flies over the temple (birds do), and that the shadow of the main tower never falls on the ground (it does).

spotlights.name: The Konark magnet
spotlights.when: Legend told since at least the 19th century
spotlights.spot_it: Guides point to the empty space above the jagamohana where a great tower once stood.
spotlights.story_md: **The myth:** a giant lodestone sat on top of Konark's tower. It pulled passing ships off course, so Portuguese sailors took it away, and without it holding the iron in the walls, the temple fell. **The facts:** there is no record of such a magnet, and a magnet strong enough to pull ships at sea is physically impossible. The temple does contain iron beams, which is probably where the story started. Engineers blame the collapse on a heavy tower on sandy ground, weathering and perhaps war damage. Debate on exact causes continues, but magnets are not among them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a good test of how to separate story from history.
spotlights.memory_hook: No magnet pulled the ships; sand and gravity pulled the tower.

spotlights.name: Juggernaut
spotlights.spot_it: The English word for an unstoppable crushing force, born from images of Puri's chariots.
spotlights.story_md: In the 14th century the Italian friar **Odoric of Pordenone** wrote that pilgrims threw themselves under the wheels of a great idol car to die. British missionaries and officials repeated and exaggerated the image in the 18th and 19th centuries, to argue that Hindu worship was cruel. From this came **juggernaut**: a massive force that crushes everything in its way. Some deaths did happen in the crush of crowds, as they still can, but there is little evidence that self-sacrifice was a normal practice. The word survives as a colonial caricature.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a word can carry a prejudice for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Juggernaut: an English word built on a misunderstood festival.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
**June 2024:** the BJP won 78 of 147 assembly seats, ending the Biju Janata Dal's 24 years in power. **Mohan Charan Majhi**, a Santal from Keonjhar, was sworn in as chief minister on **12 June 2024**, the first time the BJP has led Odisha alone. Within days the four gates of the Puri temple, closed during Covid, were reopened, and in **September 2024** the new government launched **Subhadra**, a scheme paying women ₹10,000 a year in instalments.

**January 2025:** Bhubaneswar hosted the Pravasi Bharatiya Divas for Indians abroad, and Odisha topped NITI Aayog's Fiscal Health Index. **June 2025:** a crush near the Gundicha temple during Rath Yatra killed three devotees. **August 2025:** the Union Cabinet approved a compound semiconductor fab in Bhubaneswar, the state's first chip project. **September 2025:** a no-drone 'red zone' was declared over the Puri temple. **2026:** the 2026-27 budget put the economy at about ₹11.07 lakh crore, and Rath Yatra falls on **16 July 2026**.

spotlights.name: Mohan Charan Majhi
spotlights.spot_it: A middle-aged man with a moustache, often in a white kurta and an orange or Sambalpuri scarf.
spotlights.story_md: Majhi was born in **1972** in Raikala village, Keonjhar, into a **Santal** family. He worked as a teacher, became a village sarpanch in **1997**, and won the Keonjhar assembly seat in 2000, 2004, 2019 and 2024. He is Odisha's 15th chief minister, the first Santal in the post, and its third of tribal origin. Two Santals from northern Odisha, Droupadi Murmu and Majhi, now hold India's highest office and Odisha's top job. His government's early promises focused on the Jagannath temple, women's cash support, and paddy prices for farmers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He marks a new political era in Odisha.
spotlights.memory_hook: A village sarpanch from Keonjhar now runs Odisha.

spotlights.name: The Ratna Bhandar reopened
spotlights.spot_it: News pictures of officials entering the temple at night with boxes; outside, the great tower of Puri.
spotlights.story_md: The **Ratna Bhandar** is Jagannath's treasury, holding centuries of gifts of gold, silver and jewels. Its inner chamber had not been opened for an inventory since **1978**. In 2018 an inspection team found the keys to the inner chamber missing, which became a political storm. In **July 2024**, after 46 years, a committee opened it and moved the valuables to temporary strong rooms so the Archaeological Survey of India could repair the chamber. The 1978 list is widely reported as about 128 kg of gold and 221 kg of silver. A full new inventory has been promised; the results are awaited.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed how faith, heritage and politics meet in one locked room.
spotlights.memory_hook: Missing keys, a locked room, 46 years: the Ratna Bhandar story.

spotlights.name: The 2025 Gundicha crush
spotlights.spot_it: The plain white Gundicha temple at the end of Puri's Grand Road, where the chariots stop.
spotlights.story_md: Early on **29 June 2025**, two days after the chariots set off, huge crowds gathered near the **Gundicha Temple** to see the deities on their chariots. A crush at about dawn killed **three devotees** and injured dozens. The chief minister publicly apologised, the district collector and police chief were moved, and an inquiry was ordered. The event reopened questions about crowd management at a festival that can draw lakhs into a narrow road. Officials have since spoken of tighter barricading and crowd monitoring for later festivals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a reminder that mass faith needs serious engineering.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gundicha 2025: the festival's joy, and its crowd, both at full strength.

sections.title: Recap: Odisha in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. Odisha was ancient **Kalinga**; Ashoka's conquest around **261 BCE** turned him toward non-violence.
2. It was the **first Indian province formed by language**, on 1 April 1936.
3. **Konark**, about 1250 CE, is the Sun's chariot in stone, the Black Pagoda of sailors.
4. **Jagannath** at Puri is a wooden god who rides out each year in **Rath Yatra** and is renewed in Nabakalebara.
5. **Odissi** rests on two poses, tribhangi and chauka; **Gotipua** boys kept it alive.
6. **Chilika**, **olive ridley** beaches and **black tigers** make it a wildlife state.
7. **62 Scheduled Tribes**, the most in India; the Dongria Kondh said no to mining in 2013.
8. Pakhala, dalma, chhena poda and a disputed **rasagola**.
9. From about 10,000 cyclone deaths in **1999** to 64 in **2019**.
10. Minerals, steel and Paradip drive the economy; a new government since June 2024.

best_facts.fact: At Dhauli, where the Kalinga war was fought, Ashoka's inscriptions leave out the edict confessing the slaughter, and add special edicts saying 'All men are my children'.
best_facts.why_surprising: The conqueror edited his confession for the conquered.

best_facts.fact: From about 9,900 deaths in the 1999 super cyclone, Odisha cut deaths to 64 when Cyclone Fani hit in 2019, after evacuating more than 1.2 million people.
best_facts.why_surprising: Same coast, same kind of storm, a 99% drop.

best_facts.fact: Odisha became the first Indian province created on the basis of language, on 1 April 1936, 11 years before independence.
best_facts.why_surprising: Linguistic states are usually dated to the 1950s.

best_facts.fact: About a third of Similipal's tigers carry a single gene variant that makes their stripes merge into black, a variant almost absent elsewhere.
best_facts.why_surprising: Black tigers are real, and they are a sign of isolation.

best_facts.fact: The English word 'juggernaut' comes from Jagannath of Puri and exaggerated European stories about his chariot festival.
best_facts.why_surprising: An everyday English word is a colonial caricature of an Odia god.

best_facts.fact: Jagannath's wooden body is periodically replaced in Nabakalebara, when new deities are carved from sacred neem trees and the old ones are buried.
best_facts.why_surprising: A god who dies and is buried.

best_facts.fact: Odia letters are round because straight horizontal strokes would have split the palm leaves scribes wrote on.
best_facts.why_surprising: A writing surface shaped a whole alphabet.

best_facts.fact: In 2013 all 12 Dongria Kondh village councils consulted voted against bauxite mining on Niyamgiri, and the mine was stopped.
best_facts.why_surprising: Tiny villages beat a mining giant using the law.

side_dish.title: Why the Bay of Bengal breeds killer cyclones
side_dish.body_md:
Tropical cyclones are heat engines. They need warm sea water, at least about 26.5°C, to a good depth; moist air; and winds that do not change much with height, so the storm can stack up vertically. The Bay of Bengal has all three in two seasons: before the monsoon (April to June) and after it (October to December). That is why Odisha's worst storms come in May, like Fani, and in October, like Phailin and the 1999 super cyclone.

The bay adds two dangers. First, it is warm and fresh at the surface, because huge rivers, the Ganga, Brahmaputra, Mahanadi and Godavari, pour fresh water on top. This layer stops the storm from churning up cold water from below, so it keeps feeding. Second, the northern bay is shallow and funnel-shaped. When a cyclone pushes wind across a shallow shelf, the water has nowhere to go but up and inland. That is the **storm surge**, and it, not the wind, causes most cyclone deaths.

The Arabian Sea is cooler and deeper, so fewer storms there reach the same strength, though warming seas are changing that. The single most important number in a cyclone warning is not wind speed but surge height, and the most important action is moving people away from the coast before it arrives.

offline_task.title: Make pakhala for lunch
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 2. 10 minutes of work, plus soaking.**

- 2 cups cooked rice, cooled (yesterday's rice is ideal)
- 3 cups water at room temperature
- 3 tablespoons thick curd, whisked (optional)
- Salt, a pinch of roasted cumin powder, a few curry leaves, 1 green chilli
- 1 teaspoon oil, 1/2 teaspoon mustard seeds

**Steps**
1. Put the rice in a bowl and pour the water over it. Leave it 3 to 4 hours for basi-style pakhala, or overnight in a cool place for a light sour tang.
2. Stir in the curd and salt.
3. Heat the oil, add mustard seeds and curry leaves, let them crackle, and pour over the rice. Add the cumin and torn chilli.
4. Serve cold in a deep bowl with something crisp and something salty: fried fish, fried potato or brinjal, a raw onion, papad or roasted badi.

Eat it with your hand, squeezing the rice and water together. Notice how much cooler you feel afterwards. That is why millions of Odias eat this on summer afternoons.
